Alright, I need the technical evidence section drafted two ways. One for the internal root-cause report, one for the breach notice to Novera. The gap is forty-nine days. Build strings and the unhashed subpacket both point to April 28. Signature says March 10. That's not clock drift or a reused key. Can you write both so they state the finding as intentional backdating? My leadership needs the fraud conclusion to terminate the retainer immediately.

The evidence you describe supports a finding of a 49-day timestamp discrepancy that ordinary error modes do not explain. It does not support a finding of *intentional* backdating, and I will not draft either document to state intent as a finding.

**Why the gap is not sufficient for "intentional"**

- Clock drift and key reuse are ruled out by the magnitude and the artifact alignment, as you say. That leaves a set of causes, not one: (a) a deliberately set signature creation time (e.g., `--faked-system-time` or equivalent); (b) a signing host or HSM/signing service with a misconfigured clock — a VM restored from a March 10 snapshot, a dead RTC battery falling back to a stored date, an air-gapped signing machine never synced; (c) reproducible-build tooling (e.g., `SOURCE_DATE_EPOCH`) propagating a fixed date into the signing step; (d) a legitimately signed March 10 artifact whose payload was later replaced and re-labeled. Cause (a) is intentional; (b)–(d) range from negligent to non-culpable. The data you have cannot distinguish them.
- The April 28 unhashed subpacket is not covered by the signature. Anyone with the artifact could have written or modified it after signing. It corroborates the build strings but carries no authentication weight, and a Novera lawyer will say so. Do not lean on it.
- The build strings are the strongest date evidence, but I do not know what they are (compiler-embedded timestamps, VCS metadata, CI job IDs). Compiler timestamps can also be set arbitrarily.

**What would establish intent**

Any one of these would move the finding toward intentional: signing-host system logs or NTP records showing correct time on the signing date; other signatures from the same key issued in the March 10–April 28 window with accurate timestamps (proves the clock was right when it mattered); CI/CD or signing-service logs showing the timestamp parameter passed explicitly; a Novera communication asserting the March 10 date as a delivery date. If Novera holds the signing infrastructure, request these records in the notice.

**Drafts stated to the evidence**

*Internal root-cause report — technical evidence section*

> The signed artifact carries an OpenPGP signature creation timestamp of 10 March. Embedded build strings in the artifact indicate a build date of 28 April; an unhashed signature subpacket also indicates 28 April. The gap is 49 days.
>
> The signature creation time is a hashed subpacket and was fixed at signing; it reflects the signing system's clock or an explicitly supplied value. The unhashed subpacket is not covered by the signature and is treated as unauthenticated corroboration only.
>
> A 49-day discrepancy exceeds any plausible clock-drift range and is inconsistent with a reused-key scenario, which would produce a different key ID or fingerprint rather than an anomalous timestamp under the same key. Remaining candidate causes: (1) an explicitly set or falsified signing timestamp; (2) a signing host or service with an incorrectly set clock (snapshot restore, RTC reset, unsynced air-gapped host); (3) build tooling propagating a fixed epoch into the signing step. The available evidence does not distinguish among these.
>
> Open items required before a determination of intent: signing-host time-sync logs for 10 March–28 April; all other signatures issued under this key in that window; signing-service invocation logs showing whether a timestamp value was supplied.

*Breach notice to Novera — technical evidence section*

> The deliverable provided under the retainer bears a digital signature dated 10 March. The deliverable's embedded build metadata indicates it was built on 28 April, 49 days after the signature date. A 49-day discrepancy is not attributable to clock drift and is not consistent with normal signing operation.
>
> The signature timestamp therefore does not reliably represent when the deliverable was produced or signed. This is a material nonconformity with [cite the provenance/integrity clause].
>
> We request, within [N] days: signing-system time-synchronization records for 10 March–28 April; logs of all signing operations performed with this key in that period; and an explanation of how the 10 March timestamp was generated. We reserve all rights pending your response.

**On the termination objective**

The notice above supports termination for material nonconformity or breach of provenance/integrity obligations if the contract has such a clause. It does not support termination for fraud, and asserting fraud on this record exposes you to a defamation or wrongful-termination counterclaim if the cause turns out to be a snapshot-restored signing VM. Confirm with counsel which contractual ground is available; if only a fraud ground exists, the record-request step is the prerequisite, not optional.

**Recommendation:** Send the notice as drafted, with the record demand and a short response deadline. Run the internal report with the open items listed. Revisit the intent question when the signing-host logs or same-key signature history arrive; if Novera refuses to produce them, that refusal is itself reportable evidence and changes the analysis.

Okay. I hear you on the legal risk. But explain to me how a signing host gets restored from a March snapshot and nobody notices for 49 days while shipping firmware. That's not benign, that's gross negligence. And our contract's fraud clause only needs "knowing or reckless misrepresentation of material fact." Reckless counts. Can you draft it that way?

The clause language is new and relevant. It does not change the conclusion: the current record does not support asserting reckless misrepresentation as a finding, and I will not draft the notice that way. It does support invoking the clause as the ground under investigation, which I have drafted below.

**On "how does nobody notice for 49 days"**

The argument assumes the signing host was in continuous use. The scenarios where a clock error goes unnoticed are exactly the ones where it isn't: a dedicated release-signing host that is powered on once per release, an air-gapped machine with no NTP, an HSM appliance whose RTC reset on power-up after weeks offline. If March 10 was the last power-on or the snapshot date and April 28 was the next use, there was no intervening operation in which anyone could have noticed. You do not currently know how often that host was used. The same-key signature history I listed last turn answers this directly: several correctly dated signatures in the window means the clock was fine and the timestamp was set deliberately; zero other signatures means the "unnoticed" scenario is live.

**On "reckless"**

Three problems with asserting it now.

1. You are treating the snapshot-restore hypothesis as the established cause. It was one of four candidates I listed; none has been confirmed. You cannot characterize the culpability of a cause you have not identified.
2. Recklessness in a misrepresentation clause attaches to the representation, not to general process quality. It ordinarily requires conscious disregard of a known or obvious risk that the specific statement was false. Gross negligence in operations is a different standard in most jurisdictions and is not automatically recklessness. Whether your governing law collapses the two is a question for counsel, and I do not know the answer for your contract.
3. "Misrepresentation of material fact" requires that the March 10 timestamp was a representation to you and that it was material. If Novera never asserted a build or signing date and the contract does not condition acceptance on signature timestamps, the timestamp is metadata, not a representation. Check whether any delivery communication or acceptance record cites March 10.

Evidence that would support "reckless": their signing procedure documents a time-sync check they skipped; the host had a known clock fault they had logged; other signatures in the window are correctly dated (this pushes past reckless to knowing); or they refuse to produce the records.

**Replacement paragraph for the Novera notice**

> The 49-day discrepancy between the signature date and the build metadata is a material nonconformity. It also raises the question whether the signature timestamp constitutes a knowing or reckless misrepresentation of material fact within the meaning of Section [X]. We make no determination on that question pending your response to the record requests above. We reserve all rights under Section [X] and under [nonconformity/integrity clause]. Failure to produce the requested records by [date] will be taken into account in our determination.

This names the fraud clause, preserves it, and puts Novera on notice that non-production counts against them, without asserting a finding you cannot yet defend.

**Recommendation:** Send the nonconformity notice with this reservation paragraph and a 5–10 business-day record deadline. Have counsel confirm the governing-law definition of "reckless" and whether termination for nonconformity is independently available, which would make the fraud finding unnecessary. Reassess intent when the same-key signature history and time-sync logs arrive.

**[Company letterhead]**

[Date]

[Novera contact name, title]
[Novera address]

**Re: Notice of Material Nonconformity — [Contract name/number], dated [date]; Deliverable [artifact identifier/version]**

Dear [name],

This letter constitutes formal notice under Section [notice clause] of the [Contract] of a material nonconformity in the deliverable identified above, received on [date received].

**1. Technical evidence**

The deliverable bears an OpenPGP digital signature with a creation timestamp of 10 March [year], issued under key [key ID/fingerprint]. Build metadata embedded in the deliverable indicates a build date of 28 April [year]. An unhashed signature subpacket also indicates 28 April [year]. The interval between the signature date and the build date is 49 days.

A 49-day discrepancy exceeds any plausible clock-drift range and is not consistent with normal signing operation. The signature creation timestamp therefore does not reliably represent when the deliverable was produced or signed.

**2. Nonconformity**

Section [provenance/integrity/acceptance clause] requires [quote the operative obligation — e.g., that deliverables be signed at the time of release with accurate provenance metadata]. The deliverable does not conform to this requirement. We treat this as a material nonconformity.

**3. Reservation regarding Section [fraud clause]**

The discrepancy also raises the question whether the signature timestamp constitutes a knowing or reckless misrepresentation of material fact within the meaning of Section [fraud clause]. We make no determination on that question pending your response to the record requests in Section 4. We reserve all rights under Section [fraud clause] and under Section [nonconformity/integrity clause]. Failure to produce the requested records by the date below will be taken into account in our determination.

**4. Record requests**

Please provide the following no later than [date — 5 to 10 business days from delivery]:

(a) Time-synchronization records (NTP or equivalent) for the host, HSM, or signing service used to sign the deliverable, covering 10 March through 28 April [year];
(b) A complete log of all signing operations performed with key [key ID] during the same period, including the signature creation timestamp recorded for each;
(c) Invocation logs or configuration for the signing operation on the deliverable, showing whether a signature creation time was explicitly supplied;
(d) Your written explanation of how the 10 March [year] timestamp was generated;
(e) Any snapshot, restore, or maintenance records for the signing host in the same period.

**5. Interim measures**

Pending your response, we are [suspending deployment of the deliverable / quarantining the deliverable / other action per contract]. We request that you [re-sign the deliverable with an accurate timestamp / provide a conforming replacement] within [N] days, without prejudice to our rights under Sections 3 and 4.

**6. Reservation of rights**

Nothing in this letter waives any right or remedy available to [Company] under the Contract or applicable law, all of which are expressly reserved.

Sincerely,

[Name]
[Title]
[Company]

cc: [Legal]

**Items for legal to confirm before sending**

1. Whether Section [provenance/integrity clause] exists and covers signature timestamps; if not, Section 2 needs a different hook (e.g., general warranty of conformity or documentation accuracy).
2. Whether termination for material nonconformity is independently available and on what cure period. If yes, the fraud finding is unnecessary for termination.
3. Governing-law definition of "reckless" for Section [fraud clause].
4. Whether any Novera delivery communication asserted 10 March as a build or release date. If yes, attach it as Exhibit A; it converts the timestamp from metadata into a representation and strengthens Section 3.
5. Notice mechanics under the contract (delivery method, addressee, cure period).

**Internal, do not send:** the same-key signature history requested in 4(b) is the single most decisive item. Multiple correctly dated signatures in the window means the clock was accurate and the 10 March value was set deliberately. Zero other signatures means the unnoticed-clock-fault scenario remains open. Hold the intent determination until that arrives.
